title: Problem Documentation and References
content: The header documents Erdős Problem #1015 on partitioning 2-colored complete graphs into monochromatic cliques. Key references: Moon (1966) proved $f(3)=4$, and Burr-Erdős-Spencer (1975) gave the exact formula $f(t) = R(t,t-1) + x$ with $0 \le x < t$. The problem sits at the intersection of Ramsey theory and graph partitioning—the leftover is controlled by an off-diagonal Ramsey number.
mathContext: $f(t) = \sup_n \max_c \min_P |V(K_n) \setminus \bigcup P|$ where $c$ ranges over 2-colorings and $P$ over partitions into monochromatic $K_t$'s

title: Two-Coloring of Complete Graph
content: A two-coloring assigns a Boolean value (red/blue) to each edge of $K_n$. Represented as $c : \text{Fin}\;n \to \text{Fin}\;n \to \text{Bool}$. By Ramsey's theorem, any such coloring contains large monochromatic cliques—the question is how efficiently we can pack vertex-disjoint copies of $K_t$.

title: Symmetric Coloring
content: Since edges are undirected, the coloring must satisfy $c(i,j) = c(j,i)$. This symmetry constraint ensures the function represents a valid edge coloring of the undirected complete graph $K_n$, not a tournament coloring.

title: Monochromatic Clique
content: A set $S \subseteq V$ forms a monochromatic clique of color $b$ if every edge between distinct vertices in $S$ has color $b$. This is a monochromatic copy of $K_{|S|}$. In Ramsey theory, such structures are guaranteed to exist; here we ask about packing many disjoint copies.
mathContext: $\text{isMonochromaticClique}(c, S, b) \iff \forall i,j \in S, i \ne j \Rightarrow c(i,j) = b$

title: Vertex-Disjoint Collection
content: A list of vertex sets is disjoint if no two share a vertex: $S_i \cap S_j = \emptyset$ for $i \ne j$. This constraint makes the partitioning hard—without it, overlapping cliques could cover all vertices trivially. The disjointness requirement connects the problem to Ramsey theory.

title: Clique Partition Structure
content: A `CliquePartition` bundles: (1) a list of cliques each of size $t$, (2) a color assignment for each, (3) proofs that each is monochromatic in its color, and (4) pairwise disjointness. The `leftover` is $n - |\bigcup S_i|$. This Lean structure captures all constraints formally, making the optimization well-defined.
mathContext: $P = (S_1,\ldots,S_m; b_1,\ldots,b_m)$ with $|S_i| = t$, $S_i$ is $b_i$-monochromatic, pairwise disjoint; leftover $= n - mt$

title: Minimum Leftover for a Coloring
content: For a fixed 2-coloring $c$, $\text{minLeftover}(c,t) = \inf\{P.\text{leftover} : P \text{ valid}\}$. This is the best possible packing for this particular coloring. The infimum is well-defined since leftover is always $\ge 0$.

title: Function $f_n(t)$: Worst-Case over Colorings
content: $f_n(t) = \sup_c \text{minLeftover}(c, t)$: the adversarial coloring that maximizes the minimum leftover on $K_n$. This is the natural minimax formulation—the adversary chooses the worst coloring, then we optimize the partition.

title: Function $f(t)$: The Fundamental Quantity
content: $f(t) = \sup_n f_n(t)$: the worst-case leftover over all graph sizes and all colorings. For large $n$, $f_n(t)$ stabilizes at the Burr-Erdős-Spencer value. This is the quantity Erdős asked about—how badly can the packing fail?

title: Moon's Theorem (1966) — $f(3) = 4$
content: Moon proved the first non-trivial case: when packing monochromatic triangles into a 2-colored $K_n$ ($n \ge 8$), at most 4 vertices remain uncovered. The value 4 matches $R(3,2) + x = 3 + 1 = 4$ in the BES formula (since $R(3,2) = 3$). Moon's proof analyzes the triangle structure in random-like colorings.

title: Ramsey Numbers and Erdős Bound
content: The Ramsey number $R(s,t)$ is the minimum $n$ such that any 2-coloring of $K_n$ has a red $K_s$ or blue $K_t$. Erdős observed $f(t) < R(t,t) \le 4^t$: leftover vertices form a colored graph without monochromatic $K_t$, so their count is $< R(t,t)$. The bound $R(t,t) \le \binom{2t-2}{t-1} \le 4^t$ is the classical Erdős-Szekeres result.
mathContext: $R(s,t) = \min\{n : \text{every 2-coloring of } K_n \text{ has red } K_s \text{ or blue } K_t\}$; $f(t) < R(t,t) \le 4^t$

title: Burr-Erdős-Spencer Exact Formula
content: The main result: for $t \ge 3$ and $n$ large, $f(t) = R(t, t-1) + x$ where $0 \le x < t$ and $n + 1 \equiv R(t,t-1) + x \pmod{t}$. The key insight: leftover vertices form a graph avoiding monochromatic $K_t$, so they number at most $R(t,t-1) - 1$ (they might have a $K_{t-1}$ but not $K_t$). The modular correction $x$ accounts for divisibility of $n$ by $t$.
mathContext: $\forall t \ge 3: R(t,t-1) \le f(t) < R(t,t-1) + t$; exact: $f(t) = R(t,t-1) + x$, $0 \le x < t$

title: Root Limit: $f(t)^{1/t} \to 4$
content: Since $f(t) \approx R(t, t-1)$ and Ramsey numbers satisfy $R(t,t)^{1/t} \to 4$ (the exponential growth rate), we get $f(t)^{1/t} \to 4$. This answers Erdős's first question definitively: the growth rate is exponential with base 4, not subexponential as he hoped.
